documents.title: Washington Post 'SHOP' column, Page 18 — Composing Notes / New Faces (mentions Martha Hamilton)
documents.subject: Washington Post staff newsletter column dated October 20, 1972; the 'NEW FACES' section introduces new employees, including Martha Hamilton as a News Metro reporter
documents.notes: Photo of a two-page newspaper spread; page 18 header and date visible. Top strip and inner-gutter lines are partially cut off (text of an adjacent article fragments intrude at top). The 'New Faces' entry for Martha Hamilton is historically significant to the collection. Some line endings lost in fold/gutter; transcribed with gaps rather than guesses.

Raziawi caught my attention be-" | [right top strip:] "...ost's policy of maintaining ...gements to the national ...lieved. Two in a row—it must prove oh-oh-oh! Harry Washburn and wife Ida recently completed one of my dreams—eight days in the glorious Bahamas! Harry says they spent the entire time nude bathing. (That must be what you really call 'soakin' up the sun.') The couple then spent four days at the beach in Miami. I'll wager the police were there to make sure Harry kept his trunks on—but who knows Harry, he says he went topless anyway! Joe, Joan and Frankie Rinaldi took time out recently to make a short trip to Ocean City. After arriving they met Phil, Carlene and Steve Falcone and proceeded to spend a 'glorious day on the beach.' Sam Wells would like to add his 'hats off' to the Recreation Association for the work they've done on the sports activities. He thinks it's a job well done and that each department should come out to support their team. | [middle column:] Dummy and Jane Silva spent four days at Nags Head as part of their vacation. He couldn't even discuss the big issues that just about because it rained the entire time. Brian Jacob's recent vacation has everyone green with envy. Of his trip to Germany, Switzerland, Denmark and Majorca (Spain), he said he enjoyed Denmark the most this time. He flies to Europe like most people take a 3-day vacation. | Grandfather Bert Svendsen couldn't make it to the Open House Sunday. He was helping celebrate the christening of his first grandson, Marc Christian Svendsen, Marc's other grandparents, Chris and Willo Whiffin had flown over from England for the occasion. | After the 'notorious' football game, Joe was helping celebrate the happy occasion at the home of Marc's parents, Eric and Cindy Svendsen. | Marc and Willo Whiffin—"I recently had an interesting and enjoyable experience being one of the clowns at the recent Washington Post Family Open House. It was most enjoyable seeing youngsters and adults alike join in the festivities that this occasion afforded. It was nice seeing old Post employees faces and making the acquaintance of some new ones." | "(I'd like to add to Charlie's comments—As the 'newsgirl' at the Open House I had a first hand view of all the fun the children had—and I know I enjoyed it as much as the children did. He holds a BA in drama and journalism from Syracuse University. | Rena Faglola, Accounting, Junior Clerk, is in the bookkeeping department of The Washington Daily News from 1961 to 1972. pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Paul Bluestein was paid substantially more than Hamilton and Walsh on the 1992 to 2002 salary snapshots (Walsh does not appear on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots).

Experience and Education
Bluestein came to The Post in the late 1980s as a reporter in Financial News where he remains today. Prior to starting at The Post, Bluestein was the Chief Economics Correspondent at the Wall Street Journal for approximately eight and-a-half years. Prior to his time at The Wall Street Journal, Bluestein served as the Associate Editor at Forbes Magazine for approximately four years. Bluestein is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin and has a Masters degree in Philosophy, Politics and Economics from Oxford University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Bluestein received approximately a four percent increase over his prior salary at the Wall Street Journal. His starting salary was substantially more than the salaries of Hamilton and Walsh at that time.

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, Bluestein had received six merit increases — all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these merit increases in the following years: 1989, 1990, 1992 and 2001.

Explanation:
Bluestein was paid a high salary by his previous employer — substantially more than the salaries of Hamilton and Walsh at The Post at that time. Therefore, when Bluestein began at The Post, his starting salary was also substantially more than the salaries of Hamilton and Walsh at that time.

Bluestein was the Chief Economics Correspondent at The Wall Street Journal and was experienced in matters of international economics which was considered very valuable to The Post.

Don Brazeal

Don Brazeal does not appear on any of the relevant salary snapshots and was never a reporter in Financial News. Brazeal was a copy editor and an Assistant Editor in Financial News from 1985 to 1988.

Merrill Brown

Merrill Brown does not appear on any of the relevant salary snapshots.

documents.title: Newsroom survey responses on promotions, quotas and management (anonymous employee comments)
documents.subject: Printed responses to an internal Washington Post newsroom survey, labeled by race/sex/desk/role (e.g. 'White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Editor', 'White male, Sports, Editor' — signed William O'Brien); discusses promotion practices, quotas, and the resignation of Alice Bonner
documents.date: unknown (undated; references Alice Bonner's departure, so mid-1990s era — not asserted from the document itself)
documents.notes: Single sheet, two-column layout of survey comments grouped under demographic/role headings. No header or page number visible; top and bottom edges of the sheet are cut off in the photo (first left-column heading and first lines of the right column continue from a prior page; bottom entries are truncated). Potentially related to the Hamilton arbitration background (newsroom climate survey) but carries no arbitration banner, so classified 'other'. Several line endings at the right margin of the photo are soft/out of focus; transcribed as legible.

pages.transcript:
[LEFT COLUMN] White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Editor:
It seems to me that blacks and whites at The Post share some common complaints. The lack of opportunity to move around here, to change jobs, is very frustrating. There are many people who are not interested in management positions but would just like the chance to move to a better job or even move "sideways" to a new department to use their talents in different ways and avoid burnout on the job they are doing.
People feel that you have to be "in," you have to be on the "star track" or someone's protege or pal to get anywhere here. Jobs are filled before they are ever posted and since personnel moves are made behind the scenes, most people are completely shut out of the whole process. It's a continual sore point, of course, that so many jobs are filled with people brought in from the outside; they always seem to be more "qualified." It's sort of a Catch-22: You work for one of the world's greatest newspapers and you can't get on-the-job training. If you can't learn what you need to know about journalism at The Washington Post, where can you?
In a recent memo signed by Tom Ferguson which was posted on the bulletin board, he announced some management moves and said they illustrated The Post's commitment to "promotion from within, mobility between departments, and development of people." This commitment has been mighty inconsistent and comes as news to a lot of people.
Symptomatic of this problem are the comments heard about this survey — largely to the effect of, what's the point? Nothing is going to change. It's just The Post's way of patting itself on the back for pretending to do something. Here's hoping that doesn't turn out to be the case.

White female, Editor:
At issue is not so much how The Post trains, keeps and promotes minority reporters and editors. Rather, the issue is how does The Post manage its people — all its people. I have worked at previous papers for a variety of editors with a range of management styles and I imagine myself to be a good manager of people. Accordingly, I am continually struck by how poorly The Post does in all areas of management — from hiring to training to career development.
The Post knows how to reward and how to punish; it does not know how to work with an employee to find solutions to problems that will best serve the employee as well as the paper. What is particularly disturbing to me is that I sometimes wonder if The Post truly is committed to improving its management of people. I say that because I routinely see flagrant violations of basic management tenets — i.e., reporters finding out about changes in their status through the office grapevine; people applying for positions and never given the courtesy of being told they weren't selected for the job and why; supervisors publicly badmouthing people who work for them. At The Post, it sometimes seems, such practices are not violations, but standard operating procedure.
I also would like to note my objection to this survey. It is widely perceived in the newsroom that this survey is the result of Alice Bonner's decision to resign The Post and accept a job at USA Today. A black woman leaves the paper and The Post wants to know why. That reaction suggests that the only way Alice was viewed by The Post was as a black woman instead of as a capable editor with a vast knowledge of the city and a good sense of people. Perhaps this is such thinking — which reduces people to categories — that prompted Bonner's departure and that leads me to reach my opinion about The Post management of people.

Black female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial:
Because I found many of these questions silly, slanted and ambiguous, I have declined to answer many of them [continues past bottom edge of photo — truncated]

[RIGHT COLUMN — begins mid-sentence, continued from a prior page:] ...[frag]ment ending "...Raziawi caught my attention be" [top of column partially cut off]

White male, National/Financial/Investigations/Foreign, Editor:
I do not believe in quotas of any kind. Just hire the best people for each job. A quota set up to redress grievances only creates more grievances. How many times have white males in this Newsroom been told that they won't be promoted because their [AM?]E "is under pressure" to hire someone who is a member of a minority group rather than promoting from within.

White male, Sports, Editor:
1) In summary, I would say The Post is better than most other newspapers I've been at with regard to working conditions and positions for blacks and women, but it could be much better.
2) I think the area The Post is weakest in is recruitment and training of all young reporters/editors but especially blacks and a lesser degree women. My observation, after just less than one year here, is that The Post uses a sink-or-swim approach to training reporters and interns rather than a training/nurturing approach. This is fine for those who can "swim" right away, but there does not seem to be a strong systematic mechanism for helping average young reporters/editors improve. I would be happy to share thoughts on how to improve this situation and I would be unhappy to discuss them with any management people at any time. — Signed, William O'Brien

White female, Metro, Editor:
On the subject of race, it seems to me the question is not quotas for hiring or promotions, but simply hiring the best possible people. It's tokenism to hire blacks in numbers simply because they're black. They should be allowed to compete, both with other blacks and with whites and the best one should simply be hired and allowed to advance without regard to their race.
The idea of an AME for personnel is a good one, but it should not be just to monitor the career progress of any one particular group. The problem with The Post is not racial or sex discrimination, but simply favoritism in general. AMEs have a "star" system that's reinforced by the fast-tracking of specific reporters and editors who are chosen not always because of their ability but rather because they are personal friends of are well liked because they don't threaten by having unpopular opinions.
The Post's greatest shortcoming as far as personnel matters is concerned is in assuming that certain reporters and editors want to do something. Often, career decisions are made based on what is believed to be best for the paper without any consideration for what's best for the individual involved or whether that person actually wants to follow that career path.
People often don't speak up about these situations because they feel that to do so will endanger their future possibilities for advancement or will be held against them, so they wind up doing things they don't want to do or don't believe are the best use of their abilities. There's really no unbiased person in the newsroom: that anyone can comfortably talk with about such situations.

White female, National/Financial/Investigations/Foreign, Editor:
The Post has a tremendous pool of talent in the news room, but management does not use it sufficiently. There are many editors/reporters who do not want to apply when vacancies are posted because most of them are already filled for all practical purposes as The Post goes through the motions of interviews. Managers tend to pick one or two persons in their departments whom they nurture and promote, ignoring all the other talents available. [bottom edge cut off]
